subtitle: Look beyond training to the whole model lifecycle.
summary: Pip trains a recommendation model once, then hears it answering requests all month. The visible training run is not necessarily the largest lifecycle cost. Planning, data collection, training, serving, and maintenance all matter. Suitable existing data or models can avoid new work; pruning, quantization, and smaller models need quality checks. Flexible training may use cleaner intervals and suitable hardware. Pip measures repeated inference and idle serving capacity too, comparing useful outcomes rather than model glamour. The book’s limited industry evidence makes lifecycle hotspots a question to investigate, not a universal ranking.

concepts.title: Make sustainability a planning question
concepts.body: Pip wants a recommendation model before anyone has defined a good recommendation. A teammate asks what the feature must actually do. Pip writes a useful outcome, quality threshold, update frequency, and service expectations, then compares a simple baseline. Those product choices shape every later phase. Considering sustainability during planning is cheaper than repairing a deployed requirement that creates unnecessary work. A spectacular training optimization may miss the larger source of demand.

steps.text: Pip defines the feature before building the pipeline.
Compare a simple baseline before committing to more work.

concepts.title: Collect suitable data rather than all data
concepts.body: A cart of new viewing data arrives at Pip’s workshop. Must the cinema collect it all again? An existing dataset might avoid gathering, cleaning, moving, and storing another archive—but only if it is permitted, representative, and suitable. Pip checks consent and labor concerns alongside coverage. Sustainability cannot excuse poor data: unsuitable inputs can harm results and trigger more training or processing later.

steps.text: Pip checks whether another archive is necessary.
Suitable existing data can avoid repeated collection.
Representative coverage and quality must fit the task.

concepts.title: Reduce or reuse model work
concepts.body: The larger model fills Pip’s serving machine. A compact candidate might fit better: pruning removes structure, quantization reduces numerical precision, and transfer learning adapts existing learned capabilities. Pip tests the same task quality on the intended hardware before comparing memory and energy. A reused model may avoid new training; it does not erase its original training footprint or later inference. Smaller is an experiment, not permission to accept bad results.

steps.text: Pip looks for a smaller resource requirement.
Reusing or pruning a model may avoid work.
Accept a candidate only after evaluating useful quality.

concepts.title: Training has scheduling and hardware choices
concepts.body: Pip’s retraining run can wait; a visitor’s live recommendation usually cannot. Delayable training may fit a cleaner electricity interval, with a deadline and measured checkpoints or retries. Specialized processors can improve efficiency when the workload fits. Federated and edge approaches move work and communication rather than making them disappear. Pip checks data distribution, utilization, and convergence: no training topology is automatically greener for every job.

steps.text: Pip separates delayable training from urgent interaction.
Schedule within an eligible cleaner interval and deadline.
Count communication, retries, checkpoints, and convergence work.

concepts.title: Inference can dominate repeated operation
concepts.body: The training job runs monthly; the recommendation service wakes millions of times. Pip totals inference energy and replicas kept ready during quiet periods alongside training and maintenance. Model size, unnecessary calls, serving allocation, and usage frequency can change the priority. The book acknowledges limited public evidence: a one-use research model differs from a busy production service. Pip measures the actual lifecycle instead of assuming the loudest training run dominates it.

steps.text: Pip compares the whole operating period.
Measure both before deciding which cost dominates.

misconceptions.claim: Training is always the largest ML footprint.
misconceptions.correction: Repeated inference and serving infrastructure may dominate in production. Measure the actual lifecycle.

misconceptions.claim: A smaller model is acceptable regardless of its results.
misconceptions.correction: Resource efficiency must preserve the defined task quality and applicable representation and fairness needs.

scenario.title: A greener recommendation service
scenario.context: Pip compares the cinema’s large recommendation model with a smaller adapted candidate. Recommendations refresh frequently. Both can be tested on representative inputs. Pip wants fewer serving resources without losing useful quality or excluding less common interests; model choice and unnecessary calls offer different experiments.

options.label: Evaluate and adapt the compact model
options.benefit: May reduce serving memory and repeated inference work.
options.cost: Requires a careful quality comparison and may need further adaptation.
options.consequence: The team checks common and less common cases before accepting the smaller model. It then resizes serving capacity and measures real request volume.

options.label: Retain the larger model and reduce unnecessary calls
options.benefit: Preserves an established quality baseline while targeting repeated work.
options.cost: Keeps a larger serving footprint and requires caching or freshness decisions.
options.consequence: The service avoids redundant requests where results remain valid, then measures whether the reduction permits fewer active replicas.

scenario.debrief: The useful outcome and measured lifecycle determine the intervention. Neither model size nor reuse alone establishes the full reduction.

quiz.question: A production model is trained monthly but serves millions of requests. Where should measurement look?
options: Training and repeated inference with their infrastructure
quiz.explanation: Lifecycle frequency and serving allocation can make inference a major contributor.

quiz.question: What does quantization change?
options: The geographical location of the data
The numerical precision used to represent model values
quiz.explanation: Lower precision can reduce memory and compute, but quality and hardware behavior must be checked.

quiz.question: Why reuse a suitable pretrained model?
options: It can avoid some new training work
It removes the need to evaluate results
quiz.explanation: Reuse can reduce additional training while leaving quality, serving, and lifecycle responsibilities in place.

exercise.title: Plan a lifecycle comparison
exercise.prompt: Choose an ML feature and compare two ways of delivering it. Include useful quality and recurring operation, not just a one-time training score.

fields.label: Task and evaluation threshold
fields.placeholder: What result must the feature deliver, including less common cases?

fields.label: Data, training, and model choice
fields.placeholder: What can be reused, reduced, or scheduled, and what must be validated?

fields.label: Serving and total impact
fields.placeholder: How often will inference run, and what active hardware and energy will you compare?

steps.text: Pip compares the whole operating period.
Measure both before deciding which cost dominates.
